questions.stem: A pancreatic beta cell synthesizes insulin and releases it by exocytosis. Which structures are most directly required, in order, for producing and secreting this protein?
options: Smooth ER, lysosome, and plasma membrane
Nucleolus, peroxisome, and cell wall
Rough ER, Golgi apparatus, and secretory vesicles
Free ribosomes, mitochondria, and smooth ER
questions.why: Insulin is a secreted protein: it is translated on the rough ER, modified and sorted in the Golgi, then carried in secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane.

questions.stem: "The district has not eliminated the arts. It has merely consolidated them into a single period shared by the band, the choir, and the ceramics studio." The tone of the second sentence is best described as
options: candid admiration for the district's efficiency
ironic understatement that exposes the policy's real effect
neutral technical description with no evaluative language
urgent alarm signaled by exclamation and direct address
questions.why: "Merely consolidated" and one shared period for three ensembles understate an obvious loss; the gap between the mild wording and the effect is the irony.

questions.stem: An animal cell shows no net volume change in 0.9% NaCl. It is then moved to 0.3% NaCl. Which best predicts the immediate result and its cause?
options: Water enters the cell by osmosis because the surrounding solute concentration is lower.
Water leaves the cell because NaCl is actively pumped out of the cytoplasm.
The cell shrinks because the membrane becomes impermeable to water.
No change occurs because NaCl cannot cross the membrane in either direction.
questions.why: 0.3% NaCl is hypotonic to the cell, so water moves down its concentration gradient inward; the membrane's permeability to water, not to Na+, drives the change.

questions.stem: "Our principal opposes the new schedule, but she has never taught a class that starts before 7:30, so her opinion on start times carries no weight." The reasoning is flawed mainly because it
options: presents a single anecdote as a representative sample.
assumes that whatever is popular must be correct.
attacks a position its author does not actually hold.
dismisses a claim by discrediting the speaker rather than the evidence.
questions.why: The argument never engages the merits of the schedule; it rejects the claim because of who made it, which is an ad hominem move.

questions.stem: A cell in G2 is treated with a drug that prevents assembly of the mitotic spindle. Which is the most likely outcome?
options: The cell completes mitosis but produces two nuclei inside one cell.
The cell arrests in metaphase because chromosomes cannot align at the metaphase plate.
The cell re-enters G1 immediately and replicates its DNA a second time.
Chromosomes fail to condense, so the cell cannot enter prophase.
questions.why: Spindle microtubules attach to kinetochores and align chromosomes; without them the spindle assembly checkpoint holds the cell in metaphase, often until apoptosis.

questions.stem: "School should start later because sleep is important and everyone knows teenagers are tired." The thesis is weak primarily because it
options: asserts a claim without offering a reason a skeptic would accept as evidence.
takes a position that no reasonable reader could possibly disagree with.
supports a narrow claim with an excess of statistical data.
answers a counterargument before stating its own position.
questions.why: The sentence restates the conclusion's importance instead of linking later start times to a specific outcome, so it cannot move an opponent.

questions.stem: Nondisjunction occurs in meiosis II for a single chromosome pair, after homologs separated normally in meiosis I. Which gamete types result?
options: All four gametes carry an extra or missing copy of every chromosome.
Two gametes are normal and two carry an extra or missing copy of that one chromosome.
All four gametes carry one extra copy of that chromosome.
No gamete is affected because the homologs separated normally.
questions.why: A meiosis II error affects only the two products of that division: two gametes are normal, one is disomic and one nullisomic for the single chromosome.

questions.stem: A student argues that a district's later start time improved attendance. Which evidence would best support that claim?
options: A parent's recollection that her son seems more awake in the morning.
A national report establishing that sleep deprivation harms adolescents.
Attendance data showing absences fell in the district while neighboring districts stayed flat.
A survey in which students say they prefer the later start.
questions.why: Only a before-and-after comparison with a control group separates the schedule change from other causes; preference and general reports do not measure attendance.

questions.stem: A liver cell exposed to epinephrine increases glycogen breakdown within seconds. Which best explains how such a fast, amplified response is produced?
options: A receptor activates a G protein that raises cAMP, triggering a kinase cascade.
Epinephrine enters the nucleus and directly transcribes the phosphorylase gene.
Epinephrine binds glycogen phosphorylase directly and lowers its activation energy.
A receptor opens a channel that lets glycogen diffuse out of the cell.
questions.why: Epinephrine is a ligand that does not enter the cell; a G-protein-coupled receptor raises cAMP, and each kinase step multiplies the original signal.

questions.stem: "Losing the library's evening hours is a modest inconvenience for a town where the median commute is ninety minutes." The sentence's effect depends mainly on
options: citing data the reader is expected to verify independently.
a deliberate gap between mild wording and a burden the reader recognizes as severe.
an appeal to the writer's credentials as a librarian.
a logical proof that evening hours cause longer commutes.
questions.why: "Modest inconvenience" clashes with the ninety-minute commute, and the reader supplies the severity the writer refuses to state outright.

questions.stem: Mitochondria are supplied with succinate and an inhibitor that blocks complex III of the electron transport chain. Which best predicts the result?
options: Oxygen consumption increases because electrons bypass complex III.
ATP synthesis increases because the proton gradient is preserved.
Oxygen consumption falls to near zero because electrons cannot reach complex IV.
Oxygen consumption is unchanged because succinate donates electrons directly to complex IV.
questions.why: Complex III is a required relay between the quinone pool and cytochrome c; blocking it stops electron flow to complex IV, so O2 can no longer be reduced.

questions.stem: "Testing every student to find the few who struggle is like draining the reservoir to find a leak." The analogy's weakness as an argument is that it
options: substitutes emotionally loaded language for factual support.
offers no comparison at all, only an unsupported assertion.
concedes the opposing position before the argument begins.
treats a screening measure that preserves the system as a destructive one.
questions.why: A test is a low-cost screen that leaves the system intact, while draining a reservoir is irreversible; the analogy imports a cost the situation lacks.

questions.stem: A herbicide blocks the oxidation of water at photosystem II. Which immediate consequence is most likely?
options: ATP production rises because the proton gradient becomes uncoupled.
Carbon fixation accelerates because RuBP is regenerated faster.
Photosystem I reduces NADP+ at a higher rate than normal.
Electrons are not replaced in photosystem II, so linear electron flow slows.
questions.why: Water is the electron donor for PSII; without its oxidation the reaction center cannot be re-reduced, so electron transport and the proton gradient collapse.

questions.stem: "Ninety percent of parents surveyed said the new schedule helped their child. Clearly the schedule is working." Which question most directly exposes the weakness of the inference?
options: How many parents volunteered to respond, and do they resemble the wider parent body?
Did the survey use a rating scale or open-ended questions?
Were parents surveyed in person or online?
How long has the new schedule been in place at the school?
questions.why: Self-selected respondents who feel strongly can produce a high satisfaction rate that says nothing about the parents who did not answer.

questions.stem: Two heterozygous tall pea plants are crossed and produce 400 offspring: 305 tall and 95 short. Which best explains the deviation from the expected 3:1 ratio?
options: The short allele is dominant, so the expected ratio should be 1:3.
Sampling variation in a finite number of offspring produces deviations from expected ratios.
The tall allele must be linked to a lethal allele.
Both parents cannot be heterozygous if any short offspring appear.
questions.why: Expected is 300 tall to 100 short; 305 to 95 falls inside normal sampling variation for 400 offspring, and the short offspring confirm both parents carry t.

questions.stem: "Since the district added a late bus, tardies have dropped. The late bus is therefore the cause of better attendance." The reasoning is most vulnerable because it
options: relies on a correlation observed in only one semester.
uses a key term in two different senses.
fails to exclude another concurrent change, such as a new start time, that could explain both.
generalizes from a sample that contains no students.
questions.why: Correlation permits an unmeasured common cause; without controlling for changes made at the same time, the bus cannot be credited with the drop.

questions.stem: An enzyme's rate rises with substrate concentration and then plateaus. A competitive inhibitor is added at fixed concentration. Which kinetic change is expected?
options: Vmax is unchanged, but a higher substrate concentration is needed to reach half of Vmax.
Vmax falls, and the substrate concentration at half-maximum is unchanged.
Both Vmax and the half-maximum substrate concentration fall.
The rate becomes independent of substrate concentration at every concentration.
questions.why: A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site reversibly, so enough substrate can outcompete it: Vmax is unchanged while the apparent Km rises.

questions.stem: "If the district cannot afford to heat the classrooms, how can it afford a new football stadium?" The question functions as
options: a request for information the writer does not possess.
an assertion of inconsistent priorities the audience is invited to accept as obvious.
a concession that the stadium spending may be justified.
an appeal to the reader's sympathy for student athletes.
questions.why: Rhetorical questions assert rather than ask; the point is that the two spending choices cannot be reconciled, and the audience is meant to answer for itself.

questions.stem: A single-base mutation in a gene's promoter reduces binding of RNA polymerase. Which is the most direct predicted effect?
options: The mRNA gains an intron because splicing is disrupted.
The protein gains an extra amino acid because the reading frame shifts.
The gene's mRNA is produced at a lower rate, with no change to its coding sequence.
The protein is made at a normal rate but folds incorrectly.
questions.why: Promoters recruit RNA polymerase, so weaker binding lowers the rate of transcription initiation; the transcript's sequence, and thus the protein, is unchanged.

questions.stem: "The board approved the cuts at 9:04 p.m. By 9:06 the meeting had ended and the room was empty." The two sentences work mainly by
options: citing a formal record to establish the writer's credibility.
offering a causal explanation for the board's decision.
asking the reader to weigh two competing statistics.
letting the compressed timeline imply how little deliberation occurred.
questions.why: The two-minute gap does the arguing: a decision that fast reads as one that was not seriously debated, and the writer never has to say so.

questions.stem: On an island, beetles are dark or light and birds hunt them on pale sand. After twenty years, dark beetles are rare. Which best explains the change?
options: Individual beetles became lighter in response to the sand and passed that change on.
The dark allele was lost because mutation stopped producing it.
Dark beetles moved to the sand and gradually turned light.
Light beetles survived and reproduced more, so the light allele rose in frequency.
questions.why: Selection changes allele frequencies across generations through differential reproduction; individuals do not acquire a color change and transmit it.

questions.stem: "Write to the board before Thursday. The agenda is short, the room is small, and the members count the letters they receive." The last sentence mainly
options: gives a practical reason the requested action is likely to succeed.
restates the essay's thesis in more general terms.
concedes that the board may ignore the letters entirely.
introduces a counterargument the writer will go on to answer.
questions.why: Details about the agenda, the room and the letter count tell the reader the action will have effect, which is what makes the call credible.

questions.stem: In a population of 1,000 individuals at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 90 show the recessive phenotype. Approximately how many are heterozygous?
questions.why: q squared is 0.09, so q is 0.3 and p is 0.7; 2pq is 0.42, which is about 420 of the 1,000 individuals.

questions.stem: "The plan was cheap. The plan was fast. The plan was wrong." Compared with one compound sentence, this structure mainly
options: softens the criticism by spreading it across three claims.
shows that the three qualities matter equally to the writer.
builds a pattern that makes the final short clause land as a verdict.
creates ambiguity about which quality the writer objects to.
questions.why: Repetition establishes a rhythm that the abrupt final clause breaks, so "wrong" reads as a conclusion rather than one item in a list.

questions.stem: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next. Which best explains what happens to the other 90%?
options: Most is lost as heat from metabolism and remains in uneaten or undigested material.
It is destroyed when one organism is eaten by another.
It is converted entirely into biomass at the next trophic level.
Predators spend most of it growing new tissue for the following generation.
questions.why: Cellular respiration releases much of the energy as heat, and much biomass is never consumed or assimilated, so little becomes predator tissue.

questions.stem: "My daughter lost forty minutes of instruction every morning waiting for the late bus. That is what the new schedule does." The anecdote's main limitation is that it
options: uses emotional language instead of specific detail.
describes one case that may not represent the district's students.
contradicts the writer's own thesis about the schedule.
depends on a source the writer declines to name.
questions.why: One family's experience can illustrate a claim but cannot establish how widespread the effect is; the argument needs aggregate data behind it.

questions.stem: A plant supplies carbohydrate to a nitrogen-fixing bacterium living in its roots, and the bacterium supplies the plant with usable nitrogen. This relationship is best classified as
options: parasitism, because the plant loses carbohydrate it could otherwise use.
commensalism, because only the bacterium derives a benefit.
mutualism, because both partners gain a fitness benefit.
competition, because both require the same resources from the soil.
questions.why: Each partner receives a resource it could not easily obtain alone and both gain fitness, which is the definition of mutualism.

questions.stem: "A program that meets during the only free period of the day is 'optional' the way a toll road is optional." The writer is arguing mainly about
options: how the word "optional" should be applied in this case.
whether toll roads are an efficient way to fund transit.
the cost of the program compared with its measurable benefits.
whether students ought to have a free period at all.
questions.why: The sentence disputes the district's use of "optional" by showing that a formally available choice is not a real one; the dispute is definitional.

questions.stem: A plant cell has a solute potential of minus 0.6 MPa and a pressure potential of plus 0.3 MPa. It is placed in pure water. Which best predicts water movement?
options: Water leaves the cell because the pressure potential is positive.
Water enters until pressure potential rises enough to make the cell's water potential zero.
No water moves, because a cell in pure water is already at equilibrium.
Water enters until the solute potential itself reaches zero.
questions.why: Cell water potential is minus 0.3 MPa against 0 MPa outside, so water enters until turgor raises pressure potential to plus 0.6 MPa and the cell reaches zero.

questions.stem: "The school should cut the arts budget, because test scores are what the state measures." The argument depends on the unstated assumption that
options: arts classes have no measurable effect on any outcome the state tracks.
what the state measures should be the only basis for setting school priorities.
test scores in the district have been declining for several years.
the arts budget is larger than the athletics budget.
questions.why: The premise states only what is measured; the conclusion is about what should be cut, which requires assuming measurement alone sets priorities.

questions.stem: A researcher observes that male birds sing more at dawn and hypothesizes that song attracts mates. Which design best isolates that hypothesis?
options: Count songs at dawn and again at noon on the same day.
Compare song rates between two species that share the same forest.
Record dawn song rates and correlate them with morning temperature.
Remove females from some territories and compare those males' song rates with control territories.
questions.why: Manipulating the presence of mates isolates it as the variable; comparisons across time, species or temperature leave alternative explanations open.

questions.stem: "For three paragraphs the writer praises the district's transparency. The fourth begins: 'And yet the minutes of that meeting are posted nowhere.'" The shift mainly
options: confirms the praise offered in the earlier paragraphs.
introduces a concession the writer will later abandon.
turns the earlier praise into evidence for a criticism of the district.
signals that the essay will change subjects entirely.
questions.why: The praise sets a standard, and the missing minutes show the district failing it, so the earlier material becomes the basis for the rebuke.

questions.stem: Two nearly identical salamander species live on opposite sides of a mountain range. Which observation most strongly indicates they are separate species under the biological species concept?
options: They occupy the same ecological niche on their respective slopes.
Their mitochondrial DNA differs at several loci.
They look nearly identical in body shape and coloration.
Brought together in the lab, they produce no viable offspring.
questions.why: The biological species concept defines species by reproductive isolation; niche, DNA distance and appearance are consistent with separate species but do not demonstrate it.
